closure.summary: Γ preserves a pair of points of P¹ and contains an element of infinite order: its Zariski closure is the normalizer of a maximal torus.
Γ fixes a point of P¹ and is not virtually abelian, so its Zariski closure is a Borel subgroup (conjugate to the upper-triangular matrices).
The generators are parabolic with a common fixed point, so Γ is unipotent: its Zariski closure is a one-parameter unipotent group 𝔾ₐ (conjugate to upper unitriangular matrices).
Γ is irreducible, not virtually abelian and infinite, so it is Zariski dense in PGL₂.

places.headline: Not discrete
places.detail: g1·g2·g1·g2⁻¹ is elliptic: tr²/det = 9/4 is real and lies in (0, 4), so it rotates about its axis by θ ≈ 0.46010691π. A finite order m would make e^{iθ} a primitive m-th root of unity of degree ≤ 2 over ℚ(tr²/det), so φ(m) ≤ 4; no such m has (g1·g2·g1·g2⁻¹)ᵐ = 1 (checked exactly). g1·g2·g1·g2⁻¹ has infinite order. Its powers rotate by multiples of θ, which are dense in the circle and accumulate at the identity: the group is not discrete.

places.headline: Not discrete
places.detail: g1 is elliptic: tr²/det ≈ 2.118034 (a root of x² − 2x − 1/4) is real (numerically: |Im| < 10⁻¹⁰) and lies in (0, 4), so it rotates about its axis by θ ≈ 0.48120338π. Its powers rotate by multiples of θ, which are dense in the circle and accumulate at the identity: the group is not discrete.

A finite order m would make e^{iθ} a primitive m-th root of unity of degree ≤ 2 over ℚ(tr²/det), so φ(m) ≤ 4; no such m has g1ᵐ = 1 (checked exactly). g1 has infinite order. Its powers rotate by multiples of θ, which are dense in the circle and accumulate at the identity: the group is not discrete.

places.detail: g1·g2·g1⁻¹·g2⁻¹ is elliptic: tr²/det ≈ 3.1114562 (a root of x² − 42x + 121) is real (numerically: |Im| < 10⁻¹⁰) and lies in (0, 4), so it rotates about its axis by θ ≈ 0.31243956π. A finite order m would make e^{iθ} a primitive m-th root of unity of degree ≤ 2 over ℚ(tr²/det), so φ(m) ≤ 4; no such m has (g1·g2·g1⁻¹·g2⁻¹)ᵐ = 1 (checked exactly). g1·g2·g1⁻¹·g2⁻¹ has infinite order. Its powers rotate by multiples of θ, which are dense in the circle and accumulate at the identity: the group is not discrete.

places.detail: |tr²g1·g2 − 4| + |tr[g1·g2, g1] − 2| ≈ 0.61803399 < 1. ⟨g1·g2, g1⟩ is non-elementary: tr[g1·g2, g1] ≠ 2 (no common fixed point) and neither trace is 0 (neither swaps a pair of points); a finite group would need an element of order ≥ 7 and so be cyclic or dihedral. Jørgensen's inequality then says ⟨g1·g2, g1⟩ is not discrete, so neither is the group. tr[A, B] ≠ 2 and the traces ≠ 0 are exact; the sum is compared with 1 in floating point.

places.headline: Discrete — ℤ ∗ ℤ/2
places.detail: Bass–Serre on the pair g₁, g₁·g₂: g₁·g₂ fixes one point of the axis of g₁ and moves both axis directions there freely and off each other. The map from the Bass–Serre tree of ℤ ∗ ℤ/2 to the tree is locally injective, hence injective, so the group is ℤ ∗ ℤ/2 = ⟨g₁, g₂ | (g₁·g₂)²⟩ with finite vertex stabilizers: discrete.

places.detail: |tr²g2 − 4| + |tr[g2, g1] − 2| ≈ 0.75 < 1. ⟨g2, g1⟩ is non-elementary: tr[g2, g1] ≠ 2 (no common fixed point) and neither trace is 0 (neither swaps a pair of points); a finite group would need an element of order ≥ 7 and so be cyclic or dihedral. A finite order m would make e^{iθ} a primitive m-th root of unity of degree ≤ 2 over ℚ(tr²/det), so φ(m) ≤ 4; no such m has (g1²·g2)ᵐ = 1 (checked exactly). g1²·g2 has infinite order. Its powers rotate by multiples of θ, which are dense in the circle and accumulate at the identity: the group is not discrete.

Jørgensen's inequality then says ⟨g2², g1⟩ is not discrete, so neither is the group. tr[A, B] ≠ 2 and the traces ≠ 0 are exact; the sum is compared with 1 in floating point.
